Ransomware Attack in 2018 Disrupted Pakistan’s Construction Materials Industry

ISLAMABAD, June 8 – A cyber attack in 2018 targeting several leading firms in Pakistan’s construction materials sector disrupted production and delayed major projects nationwide, industry officials and analysts recalled this week.

The attack, which involved ransomware infiltrating the IT systems of at least four major cement and steel suppliers, forced companies offline for days as they scrambled to restore critical data. According to the All Pakistan Construction Materials Association (APCMA), the incident halted operations at several plants, slowed shipments, and left contractors struggling to meet deadlines.

Zeeshan Ahmed, then IT Director at PakCem Industries, said, “Our enterprise resource planning system was locked. For nearly three days, we could not process orders or track inventory. We estimate a production loss of around 8% that month.”

The attackers demanded payment in cryptocurrency to unlock encrypted files, industry sources said. While companies have not confirmed if ransoms were paid, APCMA officials stated that most firms restored operations by relying on backups and assistance from cybersecurity consultancies.

The disruption had significant ripple effects at the time. Contractors reported shortages of cement and steel at construction sites, particularly in Lahore, Karachi, and Islamabad. “We had to halt work on the Shahbaz Avenue overpass for five days,” said Muhammad Tariq, project manager at a Lahore-based construction firm. “The delay affected about 120 workers and pushed our schedule back by two weeks.”

According to APCMA estimates, the industry suffered financial losses exceeding Rs 270 million during the incident. The association’s secretary general, Samina Qureshi, said, “This event exposed vulnerabilities in our sector’s IT infrastructure. It prompted all members to review security protocols and invest in stronger safeguards.”

Cybersecurity experts noted that, at the time, many construction materials firms in Pakistan relied on outdated software and lacked basic protections such as multi-factor authentication. “The attackers exploited remote desktop connections with weak passwords,” said Adeel Hanif, a Karachi-based cybersecurity analyst.

In the aftermath, the Pakistan Information Security Council collaborated with industry leaders on awareness campaigns and training for IT staff. The government also urged companies to report cyber incidents and share threat intelligence to better defend against future attacks.

No significant disruptions have been reported in the sector since the 2018 incident, with companies citing improved cyber readiness and regular security audits. “We learned some hard lessons, but the industry is now much better prepared,” Qureshi said.
